body:
Why Information Security Matters

Citizens increasingly use digital services for banking, education, healthcare, government applications and communication. These activities involve information such as names, addresses, identity documents, financial records and personal messages. If this information is disclosed, altered or made unavailable without authorisation, individuals and institutions may suffer financial loss, inconvenience or violations of privacy.

Information security means protecting information against unauthorised access, disclosure, modification, destruction or disruption. It applies to information stored electronically as well as information maintained in physical records.

Cybersecurity concentrates on protecting digital systems, networks, devices and the information handled through them. Data protection concerns the safeguards and responsible handling of data. Privacy concerns an individual's interests and rights regarding personal information, including how it is collected, used and disclosed.

Central distinction

Information security protects information and systems. Privacy addresses the appropriate treatment of information relating to individuals. Security safeguards support privacy, but security and privacy are not identical.

The 3 Objectives of Information Security

Information security is commonly explained through the CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability. These are distinct objectives, although an effective security system may need all 3.

ObjectiveMeaningExample
ConfidentialityPreventing information from being disclosed to unauthorised persons.Only an authorised officer can read an applicant's identity documents.
IntegrityProtecting information against unauthorised alteration or destruction.Marks entered in an examination record are not changed without authorisation.
AvailabilityEnsuring that authorised users can access information and services when needed.An online application record remains accessible during an authorised verification process.

These objectives are independent. A document may remain confidential even if an unauthorised person changes its contents. Similarly, a document may be publicly available and still require protection against alteration.

Confidentiality Versus Integrity

Suppose a confidential examination result is viewed by an unauthorised person but its contents remain unchanged. This is primarily a confidentiality failure.

If somebody changes a candidate's marks without permission, the principal failure is of integrity, even if the record is not disclosed to anyone else.

If authorised officials cannot access the result because the system is unavailable, the principal failure concerns availability.

How Different Safeguards Support These Objectives

Encryption helps prevent unauthorised reading of information. Authentication helps verify the identity of users. Access controls determine which users may view or modify particular records. Digital signatures can help verify a document's origin and detect subsequent modification. Backups and recovery arrangements help preserve access to information when the original copy becomes unavailable.

No single safeguard automatically provides every security objective. Protecting sensitive records therefore requires selecting safeguards according to the particular risk.

Prelims focus

  • CIA stands for confidentiality, integrity and availability.
  • Confidentiality concerns unauthorised disclosure.
  • Integrity concerns unauthorised modification or destruction.
  • Availability concerns timely and reliable access for authorised users.
  • Trap: Encryption primarily protects confidentiality; encryption alone does not necessarily establish integrity or authenticity.

[Sources: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, entries Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Information Security, Data Protection and Privacy: Basic Concepts

body:
Meaning and Purpose of Encryption

Encryption is the process of transforming readable information into a form that is unintelligible without the appropriate means of decryption. Its principal purpose is to protect the confidentiality of information.

Readable information is called plaintext. The transformed information is called ciphertext. Encryption uses a cryptographic algorithm and a key. An authorised recipient uses the appropriate key and decryption process to recover the original information.

Plaintext: Information in readable or usable form.
Ciphertext: Information transformed by encryption to conceal its meaning.
Decryption: The process of recovering plaintext from ciphertext using the appropriate cryptographic method and key.

Why the Key Matters

A cryptographic key is information used by an encryption or decryption process. The security of encrypted information depends partly on protecting the relevant secret keys and using sound cryptographic methods.

An encrypted file may remain unreadable to an unauthorised person who obtains a copy. However, if that person also obtains the necessary decryption key, the confidentiality protection may be defeated.

Encryption should therefore not be understood as making information permanently inaccessible. It makes information accessible under the conditions established by the cryptographic system.

Symmetric and Asymmetric Encryption

Encryption can be classified according to how cryptographic keys are used.

FeatureSymmetric encryptionAsymmetric encryption
KeysUses the same secret key, or equivalent shared secret key material, for encryption and decryption.Uses a related public-key and private-key pair.
Key accessThe communicating parties must securely possess the required shared secret.The public key may be distributed; the private key must remain protected.
Basic applicationProtecting stored files and encrypting data efficiently.Supporting secure key exchange, encryption and digital signatures.

In a typical public-key encryption arrangement, data encrypted using a recipient's public key can be decrypted using the corresponding private key. The public key may be shared, but the private key must be kept secret.

Real digital services may combine symmetric and asymmetric cryptography. The important conceptual distinction is between a shared-secret arrangement and a public-private key arrangement.

Encryption at Rest and in Transit

Data faces different risks when it is stored and when it moves between devices or services.

Encryption at Rest

Encryption at rest protects stored information, such as files on a phone, computer, storage device or server. It can reduce the risk of disclosure if a device or storage medium is lost or stolen.

Its effectiveness depends on the system's configuration and the protection of decryption keys. For example, device encryption may protect information on a locked device but cannot necessarily prevent an unauthorised person from reading information after obtaining access to an unlocked account.

Encryption in Transit

Encryption in transit protects information while it moves across a communication connection. A properly configured HTTPS connection, for example, protects data exchanged between a browser and the connected website against certain forms of interception and alteration during transmission.

HTTPS does not, by itself, prove that a website is honest. A fraudulent website may also use an encrypted connection.

End-to-End Encryption

End-to-end encryption is a form of communication protection in which message contents are encrypted so that only the intended communicating endpoints can decrypt them under the system's security model. An intermediary service carrying the messages should not be able to read their contents.

End-to-end encryption differs from ordinary connection encryption, where information may be decrypted by an intermediate service or server. Neither arrangement necessarily conceals all associated information, such as the fact that communication occurred.

What Encryption Does Not Guarantee

Encryption is not a complete security or privacy solution. It does not automatically establish that a sender is genuine, prevent an authorised recipient from disclosing information, or ensure that an application collects only necessary personal data.

Encryption by itself also does not necessarily detect unauthorised changes to data. Additional integrity-protection mechanisms may be needed.

An encrypted document can still be altered, disclosed by an authorised recipient or accessed through a compromised account. Confidentiality, integrity, authentication and responsible data handling must be considered separately.

Prelims focus

  • Encryption converts plaintext into ciphertext.
  • Decryption recovers plaintext using the appropriate method and key.
  • Symmetric encryption uses shared secret key material.
  • Asymmetric cryptography uses a public-private key pair.
  • Encryption at rest protects stored data; encryption in transit protects data during communication.
  • Trap: HTTPS and end-to-end encryption are not equivalent protections.

[Sources: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, entries Encryption, Decryption, Encryption Key and Public Key Cryptography, consulted 16 November 2026; NIST Special Publication 800-175B Revision 1, Guideline for Using Cryptographic Standards in the Federal Government: Cryptographic Mechanisms, sections on encryption and cryptographic services.]

pictures.caption: Encryption conceals information until it is decrypted with the appropriate key.

pictures.alt: Encryption protects stored or moving data. Connection services may decrypt contents; end-to-end encryption lets only intended endpoints decrypt them.

title: Encryption: Meaning, Purpose, Types and Applications

body:
What Is Authentication?

Authentication is the process of verifying a claimed identity. A digital service may authenticate a person, device or system before allowing access to protected information.

When a user signs in to an online account, the service checks evidence that the user controls the credentials associated with that account. Successful authentication establishes an appropriate level of confidence in the claimed identity; it does not prove that every subsequent action is trustworthy.

Authentication is different from merely stating an identity. Entering a username identifies the account being claimed, whereas supplying and validating appropriate credentials helps authenticate that claim.

Authentication and Authorisation Are Different

Authorisation determines whether an authenticated user or system is permitted to perform a particular action or access a particular resource.

Consider a government records system. A clerk may successfully log in using approved credentials. However, the clerk may be permitted to view only records assigned to the clerk's office. Authentication establishes the user's identity; authorisation restricts what the user may do.

Authentication: Establishes confidence in who is requesting access.
Authorisation: Determines what that authenticated identity is permitted to access or do.

Common Authentication Factors

Authentication methods are commonly grouped into 3 categories.

FactorMeaningExample
KnowledgeSomething the user knows.Password or PIN.
PossessionSomething the user possesses and controls.Registered authentication device or security token.
InherenceSomething associated with the user's physical or behavioural characteristics.Fingerprint or facial biometric.

These categories describe the type of evidence used for authentication. The strength of a particular method also depends on its implementation, protection against misuse and the reliability of the underlying identity association.

Multi-Factor Authentication

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires authentication using at least 2 distinct categories of factors. This makes access more difficult when one factor, such as a password, has been compromised.

For example, an account may require a password and approval through a separately controlled registered device. These represent knowledge and possession factors.

An OTP delivered to a registered device may function as a possession-based authentication mechanism, depending on its implementation. However, an OTP is not proof that a caller asking for the OTP is genuine.

What Does Not Automatically Count as MFA?

Using a password together with a separate PIN generally combines 2 knowledge-based secrets. It does not automatically provide multi-factor authentication because both belong to the same factor category.

Similarly, asking 2 security questions ordinarily uses knowledge factors rather than 2 distinct categories.

Protecting Authentication Credentials

Authentication safeguards are effective only when users protect their credentials. Important practices include using strong and unique passwords, enabling MFA where available, maintaining device security and refusing to disclose OTPs or passwords to unexpected callers.

Phishing messages may attempt to persuade a user to reveal credentials or approve a fraudulent sign-in. Before supplying authentication information, users should verify that they are interacting with the genuine service through an independently trusted method.

A successful login also does not give unlimited permission to access information. Services should separately enforce appropriate access restrictions.

Prelims focus

  • Authentication verifies a claimed identity.
  • Authorisation determines permitted access or actions.
  • Authentication factors include knowledge, possession and inherence.
  • MFA requires at least 2 distinct factor categories.
  • A password and PIN are both knowledge factors.
  • Trap: Successful authentication does not imply permission to access every record.

[Sources: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, entries Authentication, Authorisation and Multi-Factor Authentication, consulted 16 November 2026; Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, Cyber Security Best Practices for Senior Citizens, October 2025, Mobile Safety and Email Safety sections, pp. 2-3.]
